guides.title: First Aid
guides.summary: Bleeding, CPR, shock, burns, fractures and choking.

sections.heading: Priorities (DR ABC)
sections.body: Danger: make the scene safe first. Response: tap and shout. Airway: tilt head back, lift chin. Breathing: look/listen for 10s. Circulation: control major bleeding. Call emergency services as early as possible.

sections.heading: Severe bleeding
sections.body: Apply firm direct pressure with a cloth; keep pressing. Add layers, do not remove soaked ones. Raise the limb if no fracture. If life-threatening limb bleeding won't stop, apply a tourniquet 5-7 cm above the wound, tighten until bleeding stops, and note the time.

sections.heading: CPR (adult)
sections.body: Unresponsive and not breathing normally: push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, ~5-6 cm deep, 100-120/min. 30 compressions then 2 breaths if trained, otherwise compressions only. Use an AED as soon as one is available and follow its voice prompts.

sections.heading: Choking
sections.body: If they can cough, encourage it. If not: 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich). Alternate until clear or they go unconscious — then start CPR.

sections.heading: Shock
sections.body: Pale, cold, clammy, rapid breathing. Lay them down, raise legs if no spinal/leg injury, keep warm, reassure, do not give food or drink.

sections.heading: Recovery position
sections.body: Someone unconscious but breathing goes on their SIDE, so the tongue and any vomit can't block the airway. Roll them toward you, bend the top knee, tilt the head back to open the airway, and rest the top hand under the cheek. Keep checking breathing until help arrives. (Diagram: Rama, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

sections.heading: Burns
sections.body: Cool with running water for 20 minutes. Remove jewellery/loose clothing before swelling. Cover loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth. Never apply ice, butter or creams.

sections.heading: Cleaning a wound
sections.body: Infection is the real danger once bleeding is controlled. IRRIGATE: flush the wound with lots of clean (bottled, or boiled-then-cooled) water under pressure — a bag or bottle with a pinhole makes a good jet — to blast out dirt and debris. Do not scrub deep tissue. Remove obvious grit with clean tweezers. If nothing sterile is available, clean water is the priority; honey or clean sugar packed into a wound is a traditional antibacterial dressing in extremis. Cover with the cleanest dry cloth you have and change it daily. WATCH FOR INFECTION: spreading redness, heat, swelling, pus, throbbing pain, or fever. A red streak running UP the limb from the wound plus fever is a life-threatening emergency — get to medical care fast.

sections.heading: Splinting a fracture
sections.body: Do not try to straighten a badly deformed limb. Immobilise the joints ABOVE and BELOW the break. Pad rigid supports — straight sticks, a trekking pole, a rolled sleeping mat, even a folded newspaper — along the limb and tie them ON either side of the break, not directly over it, snug but not cutting off circulation. Check the fingers or toes past the splint stay WARM and PINK; if they turn cold, blue or numb, loosen it. For an arm, add a sling and bind it to the chest. Splint before moving the person if at all possible.

sections.heading: Sprains — RICE
sections.body: For a twisted ankle, knee or wrist with no obvious fracture: REST it, ICE for 20 minutes on / 20 off (never ice bare skin — wrap it) for the first 24-48 hours, COMPRESS with an elastic bandage firm enough to support but not to numb or throb, and ELEVATE the limb above heart level to limit swelling. If it can't bear any weight, is grossly deformed, or is numb, treat it as a possible fracture and splint it.

guides.title: Health & Hygiene
guides.summary: Staying clean, healthy and rested in the field.

sections.heading: Hands & waste
sections.body: Wash your hands (or use a clean cloth and water) before eating and after relieving yourself — field illness disables you fast. Dig a cat-hole for waste at least 60 m (200 ft) from water, camp, and trails, and bury it.

sections.heading: Feet
sections.body: Keep your feet clean and dry, and air them at rest stops — foot rot ends journeys. Change and dry your socks daily, and treat trench foot by warming, drying, and elevating the feet. Tend hot spots before they become blisters.

sections.heading: Small problems, big risks
sections.body: Keep small cuts clean and covered; infection from a trivial wound can become life-threatening. Brush your teeth (a frayed twig works) — oral infections are miserable in the field. Protect your eyes from sun and glare.

sections.heading: Rest
sections.body: Rest is a survival skill — fatigue causes the mistakes that turn a bad day into a disaster. Manage morale like a resource: eat, warm up, and sleep before you tackle the hardest problem.

sections.heading: Oral care with limited supplies
sections.body:
Plaque is a living biofilm — a few hundred bacterial species glued to the tooth surface in a self-secreted polysaccharide matrix — that begins reforming within minutes of a clean brushing. Left undisturbed 24–48 hours it mineralizes into calculus (tartar), which no toothbrush can remove; left undisturbed for weeks, bacterial acid byproducts (mainly lactic acid from Streptococcus mutans fermenting sugars) demineralize enamel below pH 5.5, starting a cavity, while a different bacterial mix along the gumline triggers gingivitis — inflammation that, untreated for years, can progress to periodontitis and real bone loss around the tooth roots. Mechanical disruption of that biofilm, not toothpaste flavor or foam, is what matters: a brush working at a 45-degree angle to the gumline in short vibrating strokes for two minutes covers the flat tooth surfaces, while floss or an interdental brush covers the tight contact points between teeth, where a disproportionate share of cavities start.

Without a purpose-built brush, a frayed-end twig (the 'chew stick' used across cultures for millennia, classically from an antimicrobial wood like neem or walnut) or a clean cloth wrapped over a finger and rubbed firmly against each tooth surface does real, measurable plaque removal — not as good as bristles reaching interproximally, but far better than nothing. A pinch of salt dissolved in water makes a serviceable antiseptic rinse that raises local pH and discourages acid-producing bacteria; baking soda brushed on damp is a mild abrasive that also buffers acid. What has no good substitute is fluoride — it substitutes into the enamel crystal lattice as fluorapatite, which resists acid dissolution far better than the original hydroxyapatite — so when a real fluoride toothpaste is available, even a smear used with an improvised brush outperforms full technique without it.

sections.heading: Skin, bathing, and washing when water is scarce
sections.body:
Skin hosts its own microbiome, and healthy skin depends on an intact acid mantle (surface pH around 4.5–5.5, maintained by sebum and sweat) that suppresses pathogenic bacteria and fungi. Both directions of imbalance cause real problems: over-washing with harsh soap and hot water strips sebum, raises skin pH, and paradoxically increases infection risk and cracking, while under-washing lets sweat, dead skin, and oils accumulate in body folds, feeding the yeast Malassezia and bacteria that cause intertrigo (a raw, often foul-smelling rash in skin-on-skin folds — groin, underarms, under overlapping abdominal folds) and folliculitis (infected hair follicles, seen as small red or pus-filled bumps, often from friction combined with sweat).

When water for a full bath isn't available, a focused sponge bath targeting the axillae, groin, and any skin folds captures most of the hygienic benefit for a fraction of the water: apocrine sweat glands (which produce the compounds bacteria break down into body odor) concentrate almost entirely in the armpits and groin, so cleaning those two areas thoroughly does more than a lukewarm rinse of everywhere else. A liter of water, a cloth, and a small amount of soap (or none — mechanical friction alone removes a large fraction of surface bacteria) covers a serviceable daily wipe-down; alcohol-based hand sanitizer or unscented wipes are a reasonable stopgap for the same target areas, though they don't replace it for more than a few days before folliculitis and odor build up.

sections.heading: Menstrual hygiene in the field
sections.body:
Menstrual blood is not more infectious to handle than other blood, but managing a period with reduced supplies raises two real risks: skin breakdown from a product left in place too long, and, for tampon users, toxic shock syndrome (TSS) — a rare but life-threatening illness from a toxin (TSST-1) produced by Staphylococcus aureus that can colonize a tampon left in too long, especially a high-absorbency one. The rule that matters is time-based, not blood-volume-based: change a tampon at least every 4–8 hours regardless of how full it looks, never past 8 hours including overnight. Sudden high fever, a sunburn-like rash, vomiting, or dizziness during tampon use is a genuine emergency: remove it immediately and seek care, since untreated TSS can progress to organ failure within a day.

When commercial products run out, a clean folded cotton cloth held by underwear or a wrap, changed as often as practical and rinsed in cold water (hot water sets blood protein and worsens staining) and sun-dried when possible, reduces harm meaningfully compared to nothing. A menstrual cup, if available, holds up to 30mL versus roughly 5mL for a regular tampon and can be safely worn up to 12 hours, making it the most supply-efficient option for extended field conditions. Whatever the method, hand-washing before and after changing is the single highest-yield habit.

sections.heading: Clothing, bedding, and fabric hygiene
sections.body:
Damp fabric against skin dramatically increases the mechanical friction that breaks down the skin's protective barrier, opening the door to fungal infection (tinea, the family that includes athlete's foot and jock itch, which specifically thrives in warm, moist, occluded skin) and bacterial folliculitis. It's also a thermal problem — wet clothing conducts heat away roughly 25 times faster than dry air at the same temperature, which is why 'cotton kills' is real field wisdom: cotton absorbs many times its weight in water and holds it against skin, while wool and most synthetics wick moisture away and retain some insulating value even damp.

Laundering without a machine still accomplishes most of what matters: agitation in even cold water physically dislodges most surface bacteria and loose soil, and a few drops of any soap lift oils that water alone leaves behind; full sun-drying afterward adds real disinfection, since UV-B radiation damages microbial DNA — the same mechanism the WHO-endorsed SODIS method uses for drinking water. Rotating at least two sets of socks and underwear, fully drying each between wears, breaks the persistent-dampness cycle even without a proper wash. Lice and scabies mites, the other major fabric-borne risk in prolonged close-quarters wear, are both killed by heat above roughly 50°C/122°F — cold-water washing alone won't eliminate an active infestation.

sections.heading: Group hygiene and disease prevention
sections.body:
Most serious illness that spreads in shared living conditions travels the fecal-oral route: a pathogen shed in one person's stool ends up, via unwashed hands, on a shared surface, food, or water source, and is ingested by someone else. This is the mechanism behind norovirus (needing as few as 10–100 viral particles to infect, making it extraordinarily contagious in group settings), most bacterial dysentery, and hepatitis A. The single highest-yield intervention is hand hygiene at defined trigger points — after using the latrine, before handling any food or water — not vague 'wash often' advice but specifically bracketing those two moments, since that's where the transmission chain actually breaks.

Shared water sources deserve special discipline: never dip hands, used cups, or contaminated ladles directly into a communal container (use a designated clean scoop, or pour) — one contaminated hand can seed an entire group's supply. Communal food should be served rather than passed hand-to-hand from a shared container. A person with vomiting or diarrhea should be rotated off food-prep and water-collection duty for the duration of symptoms and 24–48 hours afterward, since viral shedding continues after symptoms resolve — this single step, more than any disinfectant, is what contains an outbreak in a small group before it spreads to everyone.

sections.heading: Building a Field Hygiene Kit
sections.body: A small, deliberately chosen kit covers the highest-yield hygiene needs in far less space and weight than a full toiletry bag.
ingredients: A travel-size bar of soap or a small bottle of biodegradable liquid soap (biodegradable matters if you'll wash near a natural water source)
A soft-bristle travel toothbrush and a small tube of fluoride toothpaste (or fluoride tablets/drops as an ultralight substitute)
20–30 feet of unwaxed dental floss (doubles as sewing thread and light cordage)
A microfiber camp towel from any outdoor or hardware store — dries far faster than cotton and packs small
A bottle of alcohol-based hand sanitizer (60%+ alcohol) for moments water isn't available
A small pack of unscented baby wipes or individually wrapped antiseptic wipes, from any pharmacy or general store
A few feet of moleskin or blister tape and a small nail clipper, for foot and nail care
A menstrual cup or a resealable bag of pads/tampons sized to trip length, plus a spare cloth for backup, if applicable
A zip-top bag of powdered laundry detergent or a small bar of laundry soap, from any grocery or general store
A wide-mouth water bottle or collapsible basin usable as a wash basin
A distinct color of tape or a marked bandana to label personal items so shared-space gear isn't mixed up between people

sections.heading: Step-by-step: a daily austere-hygiene routine
sections.body: The routine below covers the highest-risk areas first when time or water is limited, so a rushed day still gets the protection that matters most.
steps: On waking, before touching food or water: wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, or use hand sanitizer if water is unavailable.
Brush teeth for a full two minutes using a fluoride toothpaste (or a smear if supply is limited), angling the bristles 45 degrees into the gumline; floss once daily, ideally at night.
Using a liter or less of water and a cloth, wipe down the axillae, groin, and any skin folds first, then the feet, then the rest of the body as water allows.
Dry all washed skin fully, especially between the toes and in skin folds, before dressing; damp skin under clothing is the single biggest driver of field skin infections.
Inspect feet for hot spots, blisters, or maceration, and inspect skin folds and the groin for early redness or rash while you're already there.
Rotate to a dry pair of socks and underwear if the previous pair is even slightly damp; hang the worn pair in direct sun to air out and partially disinfect.
If menstruating, change your product on schedule (every 4–8 hours for tampons, never past 8 hours) regardless of how full it appears, and wash hands before and after.
Before sleeping, wash hands again and brush teeth; treat post-latrine hand-washing as non-negotiable, even if it uses your last bit of sanitizer.

Once every few days, or when fully dry conditions allow, launder one set of clothing in soap and water and lay it in direct sunlight to dry, rotating through your kit so nothing stays worn-and-unwashed for more than about three days.

guides.title: Human Anatomy by System
guides.summary: A systems-level tour of the human body — skeletal, muscular, cardiovascular, respiratory, nervous, digestive, urinary, endocrine, lymphatic/immune, integumentary and reproductive — with exact structures, functions, key numbers and the anatomical terminology used to describe them.

sections.heading: First principles: levels of organization
sections.body:
Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body; physiology is the study of its function. Structure predicts function at every scale. The levels of organization, smallest to largest:
1. Chemical — atoms (H, O, C, N, Ca, P, K, Na, Cl make up ~99% of body mass) bond into molecules (water, ~60% of adult body weight; proteins; lipids; carbohydrates; nucleic acids).
2. Cellular — the cell is the smallest living unit; an adult has ~30–37 trillion cells of ~200 specialized types.
3. Tissue — groups of similar cells performing a shared task. The four primary tissue types are: epithelial (covers/lines surfaces, e.g. skin surface, gut lining), connective (supports/binds, e.g. bone, blood, fat, tendon), muscle (contracts to produce movement), and nervous (conducts electrical signals).
4. Organ — two or more tissues forming a functional unit (e.g. the heart contains all four tissue types).
5. Organ system — organs cooperating toward a broad function (11 systems, below).
6. Organism — all systems integrated. Homeostasis is the body's maintenance of a stable internal environment (temperature ~37 °C, blood pH 7.35–7.45, blood glucose ~70–110 mg/dL) despite external change, achieved mainly by negative feedback loops (a change triggers a response that reverses the change).

sections.heading: Skeletal and muscular systems (support and movement)
sections.body: The skeletal system is 206 bones in the adult (a newborn has ~270; some fuse). Functions: support, protection (skull guards the brain; the rib cage guards heart and lungs), movement (bones act as levers), mineral storage (99% of body calcium, plus phosphorus), and blood-cell production (red marrow makes ~2 million red cells per second). It divides into the axial skeleton (80 bones: skull, vertebral column of 33 vertebrae — 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, 4 fused coccygeal — plus ribs and sternum) and the appendicular skeleton (126 bones: limbs and their girdles). Joints (articulations) are where bones meet: fibrous (immovable, e.g. skull sutures), cartilaginous (slightly movable, e.g. between vertebrae), and synovial (freely movable, e.g. knee, shoulder — lubricated by synovial fluid). The muscular system has ~600 skeletal muscles making up ~40% of body weight. Three muscle types: skeletal (striated, voluntary, attached to bone by tendons — dense collagen cords), cardiac (striated, involuntary, only in the heart), and smooth (non-striated, involuntary, in vessel and gut walls). Skeletal muscle produces force by the sliding-filament mechanism: actin and myosin protein filaments ratchet past each other, powered by ATP and triggered by calcium release. Muscles work in antagonistic pairs (the biceps flexes the elbow, the triceps extends it) because a muscle can only pull, not push.

sections.heading: Cardiovascular system (transport)
sections.body: The cardiovascular system moves blood, delivering oxygen and nutrients and removing carbon dioxide and waste. The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump about the size of a fist, ~250–350 g. Blood flow path: body → superior/inferior vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lungs (picks up O₂, drops CO₂) → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral (bicuspid) valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → body. The right side handles the pulmonary (lung) circuit; the left side, the far larger systemic (body) circuit, so the left ventricle wall is thickest. Valves prevent backflow; their closing makes the 'lub-dub' heart sounds. Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume; at rest ~70 beats/min × ~70 mL = ~5 L/min — the entire ~5 L blood volume circulates once per minute. Vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart (thick, elastic, high pressure); capillaries are one-cell-thick exchange vessels where gases/nutrients diffuse; veins return blood (thinner, with one-way valves; skeletal-muscle contraction squeezes leg veins to push blood upward against gravity). Blood (~5 L) is ~55% plasma (mostly water) and ~45% cells: red blood cells (erythrocytes, carry O₂ on hemoglobin), white blood cells (leukocytes, immune defense), and platelets (thrombocytes, clotting).

sections.heading: Respiratory system (gas exchange)
sections.body: The respiratory system brings oxygen in and expels carbon dioxide. Air path: nose/mouth → pharynx (throat) → larynx (voice box, with the epiglottis flap that seals the airway during swallowing) → trachea (windpipe, held open by C-shaped cartilage rings) → two bronchi → bronchioles → ~480 million alveoli (tiny air sacs). Each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries; the alveolar–capillary membrane is only ~0.5 micrometers thick, so oxygen diffuses into blood and CO₂ diffuses out down their concentration gradients (gas moves from high to low partial pressure). The total alveolar surface area is ~70 m² — roughly a tennis court — folded into the chest. Mechanics of breathing: the diaphragm (a dome-shaped muscle beneath the lungs) contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs; this enlarges the chest, dropping pressure inside so air flows in (inhalation). Relaxation shrinks the chest and pushes air out (exhalation). A resting adult breathes 12–20 times/min, moving ~500 mL per breath (tidal volume). Breathing rate is driven mainly by CO₂ levels (rising CO₂ lowers blood pH and stimulates the brainstem to breathe faster), not primarily by low oxygen.

sections.heading: Nervous system (control and communication)
sections.body: The nervous system senses, decides and controls, using fast electrical signals. It splits into the central nervous system (CNS: brain + spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS: all nerves outside the CNS). The neuron is the signaling cell: dendrites receive input, the cell body integrates it, and the axon carries an electrical impulse (action potential) to its ends, where it releases chemical neurotransmitters across a synapse (a ~20-nanometer gap) to the next cell. The brain (~1.4 kg, ~86 billion neurons) includes the cerebrum (thought, movement, sensation, language — surface is the wrinkled cortex), cerebellum (balance, coordination, fine motor timing), and brainstem (automatic vital functions: breathing, heart rate, blood pressure). The spinal cord relays signals and handles reflexes (e.g. the withdrawal reflex pulls your hand from a hot stove before your brain consciously registers pain, because the circuit closes at the cord). Functionally the PNS has a somatic division (voluntary control of skeletal muscle) and an autonomic division (automatic control of organs), which itself splits into sympathetic ('fight or flight': raises heart rate, dilates pupils, diverts blood to muscles) and parasympathetic ('rest and digest': slows the heart, stimulates digestion). These two branches balance each other continuously.

sections.heading: Digestive and urinary systems (fuel and filtration)
sections.body: The digestive system breaks food into absorbable molecules. The alimentary canal (~9 m end to end) runs mouth → esophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus, aided by accessory organs (liver, gallbladder, pancreas). Key steps and numbers: chewing plus salivary amylase starts starch breakdown; the stomach holds ~1 L, secretes hydrochloric acid (pH ~1.5–3.5) and the enzyme pepsin to digest protein; the small intestine (~6 m — duodenum, jejunum, ileum) is where ~90% of nutrient absorption happens, its surface amplified ~600-fold by folds, finger-like villi and microscopic microvilli to ~250 m²; the pancreas adds enzymes and bicarbonate (neutralizes stomach acid), the liver makes bile (emulsifies fat) stored in the gallbladder. The large intestine (~1.5 m) reabsorbs water and forms stool; gut bacteria synthesize vitamin K and some B vitamins. The urinary system filters blood and makes urine: two kidneys, each with ~1 million nephrons (the filtering units), filter ~180 L of fluid per day but reabsorb ~99%, producing ~1.5 L of urine. Kidneys also regulate blood pressure, electrolyte balance and pH, and secrete erythropoietin (stimulates red-cell production). Urine drains via the ureters to the bladder (holds ~400–600 mL) and out the urethra.

sections.heading: Endocrine, lymphatic/immune, integumentary and reproductive systems
sections.body:
Endocrine — glands secreting hormones (chemical messengers) into the blood for slower, longer-lasting control than nerves. Key glands: pituitary ('master gland,' controls others), thyroid (metabolic rate, via thyroxine; needs iodine), adrenals (adrenaline/cortisol for stress), pancreas (insulin lowers blood glucose, glucagon raises it — imbalance causes diabetes). 

Lymphatic/immune — returns leaked tissue fluid to the blood and defends against pathogens. Lymph nodes (hundreds) filter lymph and house white cells; the spleen filters blood; the thymus matures T-lymphocytes; tonsils guard the throat. Immunity is innate (fast, general: skin barrier, inflammation, phagocytes that engulf invaders) and adaptive (slow, specific: B-cells make antibodies; T-cells kill infected cells; both form memory, the basis of vaccination). 

Integumentary — skin (the largest organ, ~1.5–2 m², ~15% of body weight), hair and nails. Skin's three layers are epidermis (outer, waterproof, makes the pigment melanin), dermis (blood vessels, nerves, sweat and oil glands), and hypodermis (fat insulation). It waterproofs, blocks pathogens, regulates temperature (sweating cools; blood-vessel dilation/constriction adjusts heat loss), senses touch/pain/temperature, and makes vitamin D in sunlight. 

Reproductive — produces offspring; the only system not required for individual survival. Male: testes make sperm and testosterone. Female: ovaries make eggs and estrogen/progesterone; the uterus carries a pregnancy. This is factual anatomy; for personal health questions consult a clinician.

sections.heading: Anatomical position, planes and directional terms
sections.body:
All anatomy is described from the standard anatomical position: standing, facing forward, feet together, arms at sides with palms forward. Three reference planes slice the body:
• Sagittal — a vertical plane dividing left from right (the midsagittal plane splits it into equal halves).
• Frontal (coronal) — a vertical plane dividing front from back.
• Transverse (horizontal) — dividing upper from lower.
Directional terms (always relative to anatomical position, not the viewer):
• Superior/inferior — toward the head / toward the feet (the heart is superior to the stomach).
• Anterior (ventral)/posterior (dorsal) — toward the front / back (the sternum is anterior to the spine).
• Medial/lateral — toward / away from the midline (the nose is medial to the eyes).
• Proximal/distal — nearer / farther from the trunk or a limb's attachment (the elbow is proximal to the wrist).
• Superficial/deep — nearer the surface / farther in (skin is superficial to muscle).
Worked example: describing a forearm laceration precisely — 'a 4 cm laceration on the anterior surface of the left forearm, ~3 cm proximal to the wrist crease, running in the transverse plane' — tells any clinician exactly where it is without an image. Learning these terms is the shared vocabulary that makes every later medical guide unambiguous.

sections.heading: Special senses: eyes, ears, and sensory transduction
sections.body:
The eye is fundamentally a light-focusing device wired directly into the brain's own tissue — the retina develops embryologically as an outgrowth of the diencephalon, which is why it's often called 'the only part of the central nervous system you can see from outside the body' with an ophthalmoscope. Light is bent first by the cornea (responsible for roughly two-thirds of the eye's total focusing power, since the biggest change in refractive index along the light path happens at the air-to-cornea interface) and then fine-tuned by the lens, whose curvature is adjusted by the ciliary muscle to focus objects onto the retina — a process called accommodation, which weakens with age as the lens stiffens (presbyopia, the reason most people need reading glasses by their mid-40s). The retina holds roughly 120 million rods, exquisitely light-sensitive but color-blind, concentrated peripherally and responsible for night vision and motion detection, and about 6 million cones, concentrated in the central fovea, responsible for color and fine detail — the reason you see a dim star better by looking slightly to the side of it than by staring straight at it.

The ear does two jobs with one organ. The outer ear funnels sound to the eardrum, whose vibrations are amplified by three tiny bones — the malleus, incus, and stapes, the smallest bones in the human body — across the middle ear to the cochlea, a fluid-filled spiral where a tonotopically organized membrane (stiff and narrow near the entrance for high frequencies, wide and floppy near the tip for low frequencies) converts vibration into the electrical signals of hearing. Sitting right next to the cochlea, sharing its fluid system, are the semicircular canals and otolith organs of the vestibular system — the body's balance sensor, detecting rotational acceleration via fluid movement in three perpendicular canals and linear acceleration/head tilt via calcium-carbonate crystals resting on a gel layer over hair cells. This anatomical proximity is exactly why inner-ear disorders like labyrinthitis so often cause both hearing symptoms and severe vertigo together — one organ reporting trouble from two of its parts at once.

sections.heading: Body cavities and membranes
sections.body:
Internal organs sit within defined cavities lined by thin, slippery membranes that let them move against each other without friction damage. The thoracic cavity splits into a central mediastinum (heart, great vessels, esophagus, trachea) flanked by two pleural cavities, each containing one lung wrapped in a double-layered pleura — a visceral layer stuck to the lung, a parietal layer lining the chest wall — with only a thin lubricating film between them, so thin the two layers behave like two wet panes of glass stuck together: free to slide, resistant to being pulled apart. That adhesion is exactly the mechanism keeping the lung inflated and tracking the chest wall, and why air or blood entering that potential space (pneumothorax or hemothorax) is dangerous — it breaks the seal and lets the lung collapse away from the chest wall.

The abdominopelvic cavity uses the same design with the peritoneum: a visceral layer coating most organs, a parietal layer lining the abdominal wall. Organs fully wrapped and tethered by a mesentery (small intestine, stomach, spleen) are intraperitoneal; organs pressed against the back wall with only partial covering (kidneys, pancreas, parts of the colon) are retroperitoneal — a distinction that matters clinically because retroperitoneal injuries often present with different, harder-to-localize pain than classic peritonitis. The pericardial cavity wraps the heart in the same visceral/parietal pattern; fluid accumulating there under pressure (cardiac tamponade) is dangerous because the pericardium is a relatively unstretchable fibrous sac, so pressure inside it rises fast and can crush the heart's ability to fill between beats.

sections.heading: Homeostasis and organ-system integration
sections.body:
No organ system operates in isolation — teaching anatomy system-by-system is pedagogical, not biological. Consider blood glucose after a large meal: digestion breaks carbohydrates to glucose, absorbed into blood, where rising glucose is detected by pancreatic beta cells, which release insulin — traveling via blood to cells throughout the body, opening glucose channels so cells pull sugar from blood, while the liver converts excess to glycogen for storage. If glucose instead falls too low, alpha cells release glucagon, triggering the liver to release stored glucose back into blood. This is a negative feedback loop: a deviation from a set point triggers a response pushing the variable back toward it — the same sensor/integrating-center/effector architecture recurs for blood pressure (carotid and aortic baroreceptors feeding brainstem control centers), core temperature (hypothalamic thermoreceptors triggering sweating or shivering), and blood pH and oxygen.

The clinical payoff is that a single failure can cascade across systems that look, on a textbook page, unrelated: uncontrolled diabetes eventually damages retinal blood vessels (diabetic retinopathy), kidney filtering units (diabetic nephropathy), and peripheral nerves (diabetic neuropathy, with loss of protective foot sensation) — three organ systems failing years later from one metabolic derangement. Real clinical assessment moves opposite to a systems textbook: not 'what's wrong with the endocrine system' but 'given this symptom set, which systems, in what sequence, explain all of it' — the same integrative logic used throughout this app's vital-signs and assessment guides.

sections.heading: Studying Anatomy Hands-On
sections.body: You don't need a cadaver lab to build real, durable anatomical knowledge — the tools below let you see and feel structures directly.
ingredients: A basic human anatomy atlas or textbook with labeled illustrations, from any bookstore or library
A budget plastic anatomical model — a torso, skeleton, or skull — from an educational-supply or hobby/science store, useful for feeling how structures relate in 3D
A stethoscope (any basic $15–30 model from a medical-supply or pharmacy) for locating heart and lung sounds on yourself or a family member
A tape measure and a mirror, for surface-anatomy self-examination
A reputable anatomy app or interactive 3D atlas, letting you rotate and peel back layers a flat page can't show
A skeleton or muscle-chart poster, useful somewhere you'll see it daily for passive repetition

A raw chicken leg or beef shank from a butcher or grocery meat counter, for a small home-kitchen dissection (done safely and cleaned up like any raw-meat prep) showing real tendon, muscle fiber direction, and joint capsule structure firsthand

sections.heading: Step-by-step: finding your own anatomy on yourself
sections.body: The fastest way to make anatomical terms stick is to physically locate the structure on your own body while naming it out loud.
steps: Stand in true anatomical position (facing forward, arms at sides, palms forward) and name your own planes: sagittal down the midline, coronal splitting front from back, transverse splitting top from bottom at the waist.

Locate your radial pulse (thumb side of the wrist) and carotid pulse (side of the neck), counting each for 30 seconds — note both are the same arterial pulse wave felt at two very different points in the circulatory tree.

Place a stethoscope (or a rolled paper tube) just below and left of the sternum, roughly the fifth intercostal space, and listen for your own heartbeat — nearly directly over the apex of the left ventricle.
Take a deep breath with one hand on your lower ribs, then your upper chest; feel the ribs flare and the diaphragm push the abdomen out — the mechanical process of inspiration.
Trace your tibia from knee to ankle, then locate your olecranon (elbow point) and greater trochanter (hip point felt lying on your side) — three landmarks from three different bones.
Flex a bicep against resistance while gripping the muscle belly with the other hand, and feel it shorten — a direct demonstration of origin-insertion contraction pulling two bones across a joint.
From memory, write down which organ system each of the above structures belongs to, then check against an atlas — the retrieval effort cements the material better than re-reading.

guides.title: Taking Vital Signs & Assessing a Patient
guides.summary: How to measure and interpret the core vital signs — pulse, respiration, blood pressure, temperature and oxygen saturation — plus a systematic ABCDE/AVPU patient assessment and history-taking method, with normal ranges, technique, worked examples and safety cautions. Educational only; seek professional care for real illness.

sections.heading: What vital signs are, and normal adult ranges
sections.body:
Vital signs are objective, repeatable measurements of the body's most basic life-sustaining functions. They screen for danger and, tracked over time (a 'trend'), reveal whether someone is improving or deteriorating — a single reading is a snapshot; the trend is the story. The five core vitals and typical resting adult ranges:
• Heart rate (pulse): 60–100 beats per minute (bpm).
• Respiratory rate: 12–20 breaths per minute.
• Blood pressure: below 120/80 mmHg is normal.
• Body temperature: ~37 °C (98.6 °F); normal range ~36.1–37.2 °C (97–99 °F).
• Oxygen saturation (SpO₂): 95–100%.
Pain is often called the 'sixth vital sign,' rated 0–10. Ranges are age-dependent: children breathe and beat faster (a newborn's heart runs 120–160 bpm and breathes 30–60/min). Context matters — a fit athlete may rest at 45 bpm normally, while 110 bpm in someone lying still is abnormal. Always record the number, the units, and the time. Safety note: vitals guide but never replace clinical judgment; a person who 'looks sick' (pale, sweaty, confused, struggling to breathe) needs help even if a number looks acceptable.

sections.heading: Pulse (heart rate): technique and meaning
sections.body: The pulse is the pressure wave felt in an artery each time the left ventricle ejects blood; it equals heart rate in a healthy person. Technique: press two fingertips (not the thumb — it has its own pulse) gently over the radial artery on the thumb-side of the wrist. If you cannot feel it, use the carotid artery in the neck beside the windpipe (press ONE side only, gently — pressing both or hard can dangerously slow the heart). Count beats for 30 seconds and multiply by 2; if the rhythm is irregular, count a full 60 seconds. Assess three things: rate (bpm), rhythm (regular vs irregular), and strength (strong/bounding vs weak/thready). Interpretation: tachycardia is >100 bpm (causes: fever, dehydration, pain, blood loss, anxiety, exertion, caffeine); bradycardia is <60 bpm (normal in athletes, or from certain medications/heart conditions). A weak, fast, thready pulse is a classic warning of shock (inadequate blood flow to tissues). Worked example: you count 22 beats in 30 seconds → 22 × 2 = 44 bpm; if the person is dizzy or faint, that low rate is significant and warrants medical attention.

sections.heading: Respiratory rate and breathing quality
sections.body: Respiratory rate is breaths per minute; one breath = one inhale + one exhale. Measure it covertly — people unconsciously change their breathing when watched. A common trick: keep your fingers on their wrist as if still taking the pulse, and count the rise of the chest for 30 seconds (×2) or a full 60 seconds if irregular. Normal adult: 12–20/min. Beyond the number, note effort and quality: is breathing easy and quiet, or labored? Look for accessory-muscle use (neck and shoulder muscles straining), nasal flaring, the abdomen and chest moving in opposite directions (paradoxical/'see-saw' breathing — ominous), audible wheeze (whistling, narrowed airways), or stridor (harsh crowing on inhale — upper-airway obstruction, an emergency). Tachypnea (>20/min) can signal fever, pain, anxiety, lung disease, or metabolic problems; bradypnea (<12/min) can signal exhaustion, brain injury, or opioid/sedative overdose. The ability to speak indicates airflow: full sentences = good; only single words between gasps = severe respiratory distress. Any patient who cannot speak, is turning blue (cyanosis, especially lips and fingertips), or is slipping into drowsiness from breathing trouble needs emergency care immediately.

sections.heading: Blood pressure: numbers, technique, and categories
sections.body: Blood pressure (BP) is the force blood exerts on artery walls, written systolic/diastolic in millimeters of mercury (mmHg). Systolic (the top number) is peak pressure when the heart contracts; diastolic (the bottom) is the resting pressure between beats. Technique with a cuff (sphygmomanometer): patient seated, back supported, feet flat, arm at heart level; cuff on bare upper arm, its lower edge ~2–3 cm above the elbow crease; the cuff bladder should encircle ~80% of the arm (too small a cuff falsely raises the reading). Automated cuffs display the numbers; with a manual cuff and stethoscope over the brachial artery, inflate to ~180 mmHg, deflate slowly (~2–3 mmHg/sec), note when tapping sounds (Korotkoff sounds) begin (systolic) and disappear (diastolic). Adult categories (per widely used guidelines): Normal <120 AND <80; Elevated 120–129 and <80; Stage 1 hypertension 130–139 OR 80–89; Stage 2 ≥140 OR ≥90; Hypertensive crisis ≥180 AND/OR ≥120 (seek emergency care, especially with chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or vision change). Low BP (hypotension), roughly <90/60 with symptoms (dizziness, fainting, confusion), can indicate blood loss, severe dehydration, or shock. Mean arterial pressure ≈ diastolic + ⅓ × (systolic − diastolic); MAP below ~65 mmHg risks under-perfusing organs. One high reading is not a diagnosis — confirm with repeat measurements at rest.

sections.heading: Temperature and oxygen saturation
sections.body:
Body temperature reflects the balance of heat produced and lost; the set point is ~37 °C (98.6 °F). Measurement sites read slightly differently: rectal and temporal-artery are closest to core; oral runs ~0.3–0.6 °C lower; axillary (armpit) ~0.5–1 °C lower still. Convert with °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32 and °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9. Fever is generally ≥38.0 °C (100.4 °F); hyperpyrexia ≥41.5 °C (106.7 °F) is a medical emergency. Hypothermia is a core <35 °C (95 °F): mild brings shivering; below ~32 °C shivering stops, confusion sets in, and it becomes life-threatening. Heat stroke (core >40 °C with confusion, and often hot dry skin) is also an emergency — cool aggressively and get help.

Oxygen saturation (SpO₂) is the percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen, measured painlessly by a pulse oximeter clipped to a fingertip (it shines light through the finger). Normal is 95–100%; below 90% (hypoxemia) is serious and warrants oxygen and urgent care. Cautions: cold fingers, poor circulation, dark nail polish, and strong ambient light cause false low readings; carbon monoxide poisoning causes a falsely NORMAL reading because the sensor cannot tell oxygen from carbon monoxide on the hemoglobin — so never rely on SpO₂ to rule out CO exposure. Warm the hand and retry if a reading seems implausibly low in a person who looks well.

sections.heading: Systematic patient assessment: ABCDE and AVPU/GCS
sections.body:
In any urgent situation, assess in a fixed priority order so nothing life-threatening is missed — treat each problem before moving on. First ensure scene safety and your own protection (gloves if available). Then ABCDE:
• A — Airway: is it open? Look/listen for obstruction (gurgling, stridor, silence). Open the airway with a head-tilt/chin-lift (unless spinal injury is suspected, then jaw-thrust).
• B — Breathing: rate, effort, symmetry, SpO₂; treat inadequate breathing.
• C — Circulation: pulse rate/quality, skin color/temperature, capillary refill (press a fingernail 5 seconds, release; color should return in <2 seconds — slower suggests poor perfusion/shock), and control any major bleeding.
• D — Disability (neurological): quick level of consciousness with AVPU — Alert / responds to Voice / responds to Pain / Unresponsive. Also check pupils and blood glucose if possible.
• E — Exposure/Environment: look for hidden injuries, rashes, or bleeding while preventing heat loss.
The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) grades consciousness 3–15 by summing Eye opening (1–4), Verbal response (1–5), and Motor response (1–6); ≤8 signals a critically depressed level of consciousness that threatens the airway. Reassess ABCDE repeatedly — a patient can deteriorate in minutes.

sections.heading: Taking a history: SAMPLE and OPQRST
sections.body:
Once immediate threats are handled, a focused history tells you what is going on. Two mnemonics organize it. SAMPLE captures the whole picture:
• S — Signs and Symptoms (what you observe and what they report).
• A — Allergies (drugs, foods, environment).
• M — Medications currently taken (including doses and recent changes).
• P — Past medical history (chronic illnesses, surgeries).
• L — Last oral intake (food/drink — important before anesthesia or with abdominal problems).
• E — Events leading up to the problem (what were they doing when it started?).
OPQRST explores any pain or symptom in detail:
• O — Onset (sudden or gradual; what were they doing?).
• P — Provocation/Palliation (what makes it worse or better?).
• Q — Quality (sharp, dull, crushing, burning, cramping?).
• R — Region/Radiation (where is it; does it spread — e.g. chest pain radiating to the left arm or jaw?).
• S — Severity (0–10 scale).
• T — Time (when did it start; is it constant or intermittent; changing?).
Worked example: a 58-year-old with sudden crushing central chest pain (8/10) radiating to the left jaw, worse with exertion, with sweating and nausea, on blood-pressure medication — this pattern is a classic cardiac red flag. The correct action is to call emergency services immediately, not to keep gathering data. Document findings and times; hand them off clearly to professionals.

sections.heading: Pain as a vital sign: assessment and scales
sections.body:
Pain is often called the 'fifth vital sign' because, unlike heart rate or blood pressure, it can't be measured with an instrument — it has to be elicited consistently and comparably. The most widely used tool is the Numeric Rating Scale: 'on a scale of 0 to 10, where 0 is no pain and 10 is the worst pain imaginable, how would you rate it right now?' Tracked over time in the same person it's a genuinely useful trend line — 8/10 dropping to 4/10 after treatment is meaningfully improving even though '4' is an arbitrary number. For young children or anyone struggling with the abstraction of a number, the Wong-Baker FACES scale or an observational scale scoring facial grimacing, guarding, and restlessness captures the same information nonverbally.

What separates useful pain assessment from a throwaway number is asking about character and trajectory using OPQRST, and specifically watching for pain disproportionate to what you can see (a classic early sign of compartment syndrome, mesenteric ischemia, or necrotizing infection, where tissue damage outpaces visible signs), or pain unrelieved by rest and position change. Because pain has real physiologic effects — raising heart rate and blood pressure through sympathetic activation, and causing shallow guarded breathing that predisposes to pneumonia after injury — treating pain adequately isn't a comfort measure layered on top of 'real' care; it's part of preventing a second, physiologic problem from the first.

sections.heading: Vital signs across the lifespan: pediatric and elderly considerations
sections.body:
Adult 'normal ranges' don't apply to children, and using them on a child is a common, dangerous error. A newborn's normal heart rate runs 100–160 beats per minute (serious tachycardia in an adult) and respiratory rate 30–60 breaths per minute; both fall steadily through childhood, reaching adult ranges only in the early teens. A child's heart is smaller with less ability to increase stroke volume, so it compensates for demand mainly by beating faster rather than harder, and a proportionally larger surface area and metabolic rate drive faster baseline breathing. Blood pressure cuffs must be correctly sized (too large under-reads, too small over-reads), and a normal systolic under 90 mmHg in a young child can be entirely normal — alarming in an adult.

Older adults often run vital signs that look concerning by adult-textbook standards, or conversely look falsely reassuring while genuinely deteriorating. Resting heart rate doesn't reliably rise with age, but maximum achievable rate under stress falls (roughly 220 minus age), meaning an older adult in serious trouble may be unable to mount the tachycardia a younger person would show for the same insult. Many older adults run a higher baseline blood pressure, take medications (particularly beta-blockers) blunting the heart-rate response to illness, and can develop serious infection with blunted or absent fever due to a weaker aged inflammatory response — a normal temperature does not rule out sepsis the way it more reliably would in someone younger.

sections.heading: Trending vital signs and recognizing deterioration
sections.body:
A single set of vital signs is a snapshot; a series over time is a trend line, and trend lines catch deterioration a snapshot can miss. A patient can show a 'normal' 110/70 at hour one and the same 'normal' 110/70 at hour three while actively dying in between if their baseline was 150/90 — the number never left a technically-fine range, but the 40-point drop is exactly the signature of early compensated shock, where the body clamps down peripheral vessels hard enough to hold pressure steady even as the underlying problem worsens. Serial vital signs — every 5–15 minutes in an unstable patient, or at minimum before and after any intervention — catch problems a single careful reading cannot.

One simple calculable early-warning number is the shock index: heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure. A normal adult runs around 0.5–0.7 (heart rate 75 over systolic 120 gives 0.625). A shock index above 0.9–1.0 (heart rate 110 with systolic 100, giving 1.1) flags significant blood loss or shock even when the systolic alone still looks only mildly low, because it catches a rising heart rate and falling pressure working together rather than judging either in isolation. More formal hospital early-warning scores, summing points across respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, and consciousness level, use the same principle: no single vital sign is as informative as the combined trend across several, compared against that person's own baseline.

sections.heading: Assembling a Basic Assessment Kit
sections.body: A handful of inexpensive tools let you take every vital sign covered in this guide to a real clinical standard.
ingredients: A manual blood pressure cuff (sphygmomanometer) with a stethoscope, or an automatic digital cuff, from any pharmacy or medical-supply store — matched in size to the arm it'll be used on
A basic dual-head stethoscope ($15–30) for pulse, lung, and heart-sound checks
A fingertip pulse oximeter, an inexpensive clip-on device from any pharmacy, for oxygen saturation and pulse rate
A digital oral/axillary thermometer, or a no-contact forehead thermometer
A watch or phone with a visible seconds display, for timing pulse and respiratory counts
A small penlight, for pupil checks as part of a neurological exam
A notepad or phone note kept specifically for logging serial vital signs with timestamps
A printed 0–10 numeric pain-scale card, or a Wong-Baker FACES scale, freely available from public health sources

sections.heading: Step-by-step: a complete practice assessment
sections.body: Run this full sequence on a willing family member or friend, record every number with a timestamp, and repeat it a few days later — the goal is comfort with technique and a real baseline for comparison.
steps: Have your subject sit quietly for at least 5 minutes before starting (activity, caffeine, and talking all skew the numbers) and record the time.
Count respiratory rate first, before they know you're doing it — watch chest rise for 30 seconds and double it, noting rhythm and effort.
Take a radial pulse for 30 seconds and double it, noting rhythm and strength alongside the rate.

Apply the blood pressure cuff to a bare upper arm at heart level, inflate about 30 mmHg above expected systolic, and slowly release, noting the systolic (first sound) and diastolic (sound disappears) — or use an automatic cuff.
Clip on a pulse oximeter, let it settle 15–30 seconds, and record both oxygen saturation and pulse rate, cross-checking against your manual pulse count.
Take a temperature reading, noting which method was used since normal ranges shift slightly between them.
Ask them to rate any current discomfort 0–10, and if there is any, run through OPQRST as practice.
Do a quick AVPU check: confirm they're oriented to person, place, and roughly the time, and note it as 'A, alert and oriented.'
Write every number down with the timestamp in one place, then repeat the whole sequence on a different day and compare what stayed the same and what shifted.

guides.title: Common Illnesses & Red Flags to Act On
guides.summary: A field guide to everyday illnesses — respiratory infections, gastrointestinal upset and dehydration, headaches, fever — and the specific 'red-flag' warning signs that mean stop-and-get-emergency-help now, including stroke (FAST), heart attack, sepsis and anaphylaxis. Educational and non-prescriptive; when in doubt, seek professional care.

sections.heading: How to think about symptoms and severity
sections.body: A symptom is what a person feels and reports (headache, nausea); a sign is what you can observe or measure (fever, rash, fast pulse). Most illnesses are self-limiting — they resolve on their own with rest, fluids and time. The critical skill is triage: sorting the minor from the dangerous. Three questions guide it: (1) How fast did it come on? Sudden, severe symptoms (worst-ever headache, sudden weakness, crushing chest pain) are far more concerning than a slow build. (2) Is it getting worse over time, or better? (3) Are there red flags — specific danger signs that override reassurance. General red flags that apply to almost any illness: difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion or a drop in alertness, a stiff neck with fever, a rash that does not fade when pressed (does not blanch), inability to keep any fluids down, severe unrelenting pain, fainting, or a feeling of impending doom. In infants: poor feeding, no wet diapers, a bulging or sunken soft spot, floppiness, or a high-pitched cry. Anyone at the extremes of age, pregnant, or with a weakened immune system (diabetes, cancer treatment, immune-suppressing drugs) can deteriorate faster and with subtler signs, so lower your threshold to seek help.

sections.heading: Respiratory illness: colds, flu, and pneumonia
sections.body: The common cold is a viral upper-airway infection: runny/stuffy nose, sore throat, mild cough, sneezing, usually no or low fever, peaking around day 2–3 and resolving in ~7–10 days. Influenza ('the flu') hits harder and faster: abrupt high fever (often 38.5–40 °C), body aches, headache, dry cough, and profound fatigue. Both are viral, so antibiotics do NOT help; care is supportive — rest, fluids, and fever/pain relief. The danger is lower-airway or secondary infection. Pneumonia (infection of the lung tissue itself) is suggested by: a productive cough (yellow/green/rust-colored phlegm), a fever that returns or worsens after a few days ('double-worsening'), sharp chest pain worse on breathing in (pleuritic pain), and — the key sign — shortness of breath or fast breathing (>20–24/min). Red flags requiring urgent care: breathing rate over ~24–30/min, SpO₂ below 92%, blue lips/fingertips (cyanosis), confusion, chest pain, coughing blood, or inability to complete a sentence in one breath. Worked example: a person 5 days into a 'cold' who suddenly spikes a fever, breathes 28/min, and reads SpO₂ 89% has crossed from a self-limiting cold into probable pneumonia — this needs medical evaluation, not more bed rest.

sections.heading: Gastrointestinal illness and dehydration
sections.body: Acute gastroenteritis ('stomach flu,' usually viral) causes vomiting, watery diarrhea, cramps and sometimes low fever; it typically resolves in 1–3 days. The real threat is dehydration from fluid loss, especially in the very young, the elderly, and in hot climates. Signs of dehydration progress: thirst and dark, scanty urine (mild) → dry mouth, sunken eyes, no tears, skin that 'tents' when pinched, fast pulse, lightheadedness on standing (moderate) → confusion, no urine for 8+ hours, weak rapid pulse, cool mottled skin (severe — an emergency). Home rehydration is the cornerstone: an oral rehydration solution (ORS) replaces water and the electrolytes/glucose that drive absorption. A safe household ORS recipe: 1 liter of clean/boiled-then-cooled water + 6 level teaspoons (~30 g) sugar + ½ level teaspoon (~2.5 g) salt — this approximates the WHO ratio; do not exceed the salt or it worsens dehydration. Sip small amounts frequently (e.g. 5–10 mL every few minutes) even if vomiting. Red flags that mean seek care: blood in vomit or stool, black tarry stool, severe or localized constant abdominal pain (especially lower-right, which can signal appendicitis), a rigid board-like belly, high fever, signs of severe dehydration, or symptoms lasting beyond a few days. Avoid anti-diarrheal drugs when there is high fever or bloody stool, as they can trap the infection.

sections.heading: Headaches and neurological red flags (stroke: FAST)
sections.body:
Most headaches are benign: tension-type (a dull, band-like tightness, often from stress, poor posture, dehydration, eye strain) and migraine (throbbing, usually one-sided, with nausea, light/sound sensitivity, sometimes preceded by visual 'aura'). These respond to rest, hydration, and over-the-counter analgesics. But certain features are red flags for a dangerous cause: a sudden 'thunderclap' headache reaching maximum intensity in seconds (possible brain bleed); the 'worst headache of my life'; headache with fever AND a stiff neck (possible meningitis — especially with a non-blanching rash); headache with confusion, seizure, weakness, or vision loss; a new headache after age 50 or after a head injury; or one that steadily worsens over days. STROKE is the neurological emergency to recognize instantly using FAST:
• F — Face drooping (ask them to smile; is one side lower?).
• A — Arm weakness (ask them to raise both arms; does one drift down?).
• S — Speech difficulty (slurred, garbled, or unable to repeat a simple sentence?).
• T — Time to call emergency services immediately, and note the exact time symptoms began.
Stroke treatments are time-critical — 'time is brain,' with roughly 1.9 million neurons lost per minute — so never 'wait and see.' Other stroke signs: sudden numbness (especially one-sided), sudden severe dizziness or loss of balance, and sudden vision loss.

sections.heading: Fever: what it is and how to manage it
sections.body: Fever is a regulated rise in the body's temperature set-point (≥38 °C / 100.4 °F), usually the immune system's response to infection — it is a symptom, not a disease, and moderate fever itself helps fight infection. The height of a fever correlates poorly with how dangerous the illness is; a person's overall appearance and behavior matter more than the exact number. Supportive management: rest; drink plenty of fluids (fever increases fluid needs); dress lightly; keep the room comfortable. Antipyretic medicines (acetaminophen/paracetamol or ibuprofen — see the Medicines guide for doses and cautions) can improve comfort but are not mandatory if the person is comfortable. Do NOT sponge with cold water or alcohol (causes shivering, which raises temperature, and alcohol can be absorbed); use lukewarm water only if needed. Never give aspirin to children or teens with a viral illness (risk of Reye syndrome, a rare but severe liver/brain condition). Red flags with fever: temperature ≥40 °C (104 °F) not responding to measures; fever with a stiff neck, severe headache, or a non-blanching rash; fever with breathing difficulty, chest pain, or confusion; any fever in an infant under 3 months (an emergency — get care immediately); fever lasting more than ~3–5 days; or fever in someone immunocompromised. Febrile seizures can occur in young children; keep them safe from injury, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, time the seizure, and seek care.

sections.heading: Chest pain, heart attack, and cardiac red flags
sections.body: Chest pain has many causes — muscular strain, acid reflux (burning behind the breastbone, often after meals or lying down), anxiety, or lung problems — but heart attack (myocardial infarction) must be ruled out first because it is time-critical. Classic cardiac warning signs: pressure, squeezing, tightness, or a heavy 'crushing' feeling in the center or left chest lasting more than a few minutes or coming and going; pain radiating to the left arm, jaw, neck, back, or upper abdomen; accompanied by shortness of breath, cold sweat, nausea, lightheadedness, or a sense of doom. Important: women, older adults, and people with diabetes often have atypical presentations — fatigue, shortness of breath, jaw or back discomfort, or indigestion-like symptoms rather than dramatic chest pain — so do not dismiss these. Action for suspected heart attack: call emergency services immediately; have the person sit and rest; loosen tight clothing; if they are not allergic and it is locally advised, they may chew one adult aspirin (typically 300–325 mg) to thin the blood — but calling for help comes first. Be ready to perform CPR if the person collapses and is not breathing normally: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, ~100–120 compressions/min, ~5–6 cm deep, and use an automated external defibrillator (AED) if available. Distinguish reflux by its burning quality and response to antacids, but when uncertain, treat chest pain as cardiac until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: Serious systemic red flags: sepsis and anaphylaxis
sections.body:
Two life-threatening emergencies can arise from otherwise ordinary triggers, and recognizing them fast saves lives.

Sepsis is the body's overwhelming, dysregulated response to an infection, causing organ dysfunction; it can follow any infection (chest, urine, skin, gut). Warning signs (mnemonic SEPSIS-like): Slurred speech or new confusion; Extreme shivering or muscle pain; Passing no urine in a day; Severe breathlessness; feeling like 'I might die'; Skin that is mottled, bluish, pale, or blotchy. Other clues: a fever OR an abnormally low temperature, a fast heart rate (>90–100), fast breathing, and clammy skin. Sepsis is a medical emergency — seek care immediately and say the word 'sepsis'; early antibiotics and fluids are decisive.

Anaphylaxis is a severe, rapid allergic reaction (to foods like nuts/shellfish, insect stings, medications, latex) that can kill within minutes. It typically involves two or more body systems: skin (hives, flushing, swelling of lips/tongue/throat), breathing (wheeze, stridor, tightness, difficulty breathing), circulation (dizziness, fainting, collapse from a drop in blood pressure), and gut (vomiting, cramps). Action: use an adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector without delay if available and prescribed — inject into the outer mid-thigh — then call emergency services; a person can lie down with legs raised (or sit up if breathing is hard); a second dose may be needed after ~5 minutes if no improvement. Antihistamines and inhalers are NOT substitutes for adrenaline in true anaphylaxis. Any of these systemic red flags means act first, gather details later.

sections.heading: Skin infections and dangerous rashes
sections.body:
Most skin redness is benign, but a small set of patterns separate ordinary irritation from something urgent. Cellulitis — bacterial infection of the skin and tissue just beneath it, usually Streptococcus or Staphylococcus entering through a break in the skin — presents as red, warm, swollen, tender skin with a poorly defined border spreading over hours to days; marking the edge with a pen and rechecking in a few hours is a genuinely useful way to see whether it's advancing despite treatment. An abscess is different: a localized, fluctuant, painful lump with a pocket of pus, usually needing drainage rather than antibiotics alone. Far more dangerous is necrotizing fasciitis — a rapidly spreading deep-tissue infection that can travel faster than skin changes suggest — flagged by pain strikingly out of proportion to how mild the skin looks, skin progressing from red to dusky purple or blistering/blackening, numbness in the area (as infection destroys the nerves), and a patient disproportionately sick — high fever, confusion, rapid heart rate — for what looks like a skin problem. This is a true surgical emergency; the infection can advance inches per hour.

A separate red flag is a rash that doesn't blanch (turn white) under pressure — press a clear glass or a finger firmly, and if discoloration stays visible, that's non-blanching, classically from bleeding under the skin (petechiae or purpura) rather than dilated vessels. In someone also feverish with a severe headache or neck stiffness, a non-blanching rash is a hallmark warning sign of meningococcemia — bacteria in the bloodstream — a medical emergency regardless of how the person otherwise looks, since this infection can go from mild symptoms to septic shock within hours. Ordinary allergic or viral rashes, by contrast, are typically blanching, itchy rather than painful, in someone who otherwise looks reasonably well.

sections.heading: Abdominal pain: the acute abdomen and its red flags
sections.body:
Abdominal pain is hard to triage from the outside because so many organs can cause it, but a few exam findings reliably separate concerning from watch-and-wait. Guarding — reflexive muscle tensing when pressed, distinct from simple tenderness — and its more serious cousin rigidity (the wall board-hard even at rest) signal peritoneal irritation, typically from infection, perforation, or bleeding. Rebound tenderness — pain worse on releasing pressure than applying it — is a classic sign of the same, since the wall snapping back stretches an already-inflamed peritoneum. Any of these, especially with fever, vomiting, or an inability to lie still (peritonitis patients typically want to stay motionless, unlike, say, kidney-stone pain, where people writhe and can't get comfortable), warrants urgent evaluation.

Location carries diagnostic weight: pain starting vaguely around the navel and migrating over 12–24 hours to the right lower quadrant, at McBurney's point (about a third of the way from hip bone to navel), is classic appendicitis, which can rupture within roughly 48–72 hours if untreated, turning a contained infection into diffuse peritonitis. Right-upper-quadrant pain after a fatty meal, radiating to the right shoulder blade, points toward the gallbladder. Severe pain radiating through to the back, in someone with heavy alcohol use or gallstones, raises concern for pancreatitis. Abdominal pain that is severe, progressively worsening, accompanied by fever or persistent vomiting, or paired with a rigid or exquisitely tender belly on exam should be treated as an emergency.

sections.heading: Urinary tract infections and when they become an emergency
sections.body:
A urinary tract infection (UTI) most often starts in the bladder — burning with urination, frequent urge to go, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, mild lower abdominal discomfort — and at that stage is uncomfortable but rarely dangerous, treatable with oral antibiotics covering the most common culprit, E. coli, which ascends from its normal home in the gut. The genuine red flag is when infection climbs from the bladder up to the kidney — pyelonephritis — marked by bladder symptoms plus fever (often high, with shaking chills), flank pain (typically in the back, just below the ribs, often one-sided), nausea and vomiting, and a person who looks considerably sicker than a simple bladder infection would explain. A useful bedside check is costovertebral angle tenderness: a firm, gentle thump with the side of a fist over the angle where the lowest rib meets the spine — sharp pain there points toward kidney involvement.

Pyelonephritis matters because an infected kidney is a direct route into the bloodstream, and untreated it can progress to bacteremia and sepsis within days. It's treated more aggressively than a bladder infection — a longer course, sometimes IV antibiotics and admission if vomiting prevents oral medication, if pregnant, elderly, or showing any sign of sepsis. Recurrent UTIs, visible blood in urine, or UTI symptoms in a man (structurally far less common, since the male urethra is much longer, and when it occurs it's more often linked to an enlarged prostate or a stone) are all reasons to seek proper evaluation rather than repeat self-treatment.

sections.heading: A Home Illness-Monitoring Kit
sections.body: These tools let you objectively track the difference between 'feels bad' and 'is actually getting worse' — the distinction this whole guide is built around.
ingredients: A digital thermometer (oral/axillary or no-contact forehead type, from any pharmacy) for tracking fever trends rather than a single reading
A fingertip pulse oximeter, to catch falling oxygen saturation in respiratory illness before breathing looks obviously labored
A basic blood pressure cuff, useful for tracking dehydration (a falling blood pressure with a rising heart rate on standing) and general deterioration
A clear drinking glass, for the 'glass test' on a suspicious rash
A permanent marker, for outlining the edge of a spreading area of redness so you can objectively see whether it's advancing
An oral rehydration solution packet, or the ingredients to make one (clean water, sugar, and salt in a standard ratio — pre-made packets are widely sold at any pharmacy or grocery store)
A written symptom log (paper or phone note) with columns for time, temperature, heart rate, and a short symptom description

sections.heading: Step-by-step: building your own symptom-triage habit
sections.body: The best way to internalize red flags is to practice the checks below on yourself or a family member the next time anyone has a minor illness, building the muscle memory before you need it under pressure.
steps: The next time someone has a fever, take and log their temperature every 4–6 hours rather than once, and note whether it's trending up, flat, or down over the day.

Practice the FAST stroke check as a dry run on a healthy family member: ask them to smile (Face), raise both arms (Arms), and repeat a sentence (Speech), so the sequence is automatic if you ever need it for real.

If anyone has a rash, do the glass test: press a clear glass firmly against it and watch whether the color disappears (blanching, reassuring) or stays visible (non-blanching, a red flag if paired with fever).
Practice checking for abdominal guarding on a healthy volunteer: press gently on each of the four abdominal quadrants and feel for reflexive muscle tensing.
Time how long it takes a family member to rehydrate after exercise using an oral rehydration mix versus plain water, to build a feel for how GI fluid losses differ from ordinary thirst.
Write a one-page red-flags cheat sheet in your own words summarizing FAST, sepsis, anaphylaxis, and chest-pain warning signs, and put it somewhere visible.
Review your household's known allergies and physically locate any epinephrine auto-injector now, before an emergency, so no one is searching for it during one.

guides.title: Deep Wound Care, Bleeding Control & Infection
guides.summary: A practical, step-by-step reference for controlling bleeding (direct pressure, wound packing, tourniquets), cleaning and irrigating wounds, deciding on closure and dressings, and recognizing and managing wound infection and tetanus risk — with specific pressures, volumes, times and a worked example. Educational only; deep or serious wounds need professional care.

sections.heading: Wound types and the four phases of healing
sections.body:
A wound is a break in the skin or underlying tissue. Common types: abrasion (scrape, superficial); laceration (a cut/tear with irregular edges); incision (clean-edged cut); puncture (deep and narrow, e.g. a nail — high infection risk because contamination is driven deep and it drains poorly); avulsion (tissue torn away); and amputation. Healing proceeds in four overlapping phases, and understanding them explains every care decision:
1. Hemostasis (seconds–minutes): vessels constrict and platelets plus the clotting cascade form a clot to stop bleeding.
2. Inflammation (day 0–~3): redness, warmth, swelling and pain as white cells clean debris and bacteria — some redness here is normal, not yet infection.
3. Proliferation (~day 3–21): new tissue (pink 'granulation' tissue), new blood vessels, and fresh skin (epithelialization) fill and cover the wound; collagen is laid down.
4. Remodeling/maturation (~3 weeks to 1–2 years): collagen reorganizes and the scar strengthens, ultimately reaching only ~80% of original skin strength.
Good care simply protects and supports this natural sequence: stop the bleeding, remove contamination, keep the wound clean and appropriately moist, and watch for infection. Factors that slow healing: poor blood supply, diabetes, smoking, poor nutrition (protein, vitamin C and zinc matter), advanced age, and infection.

sections.heading: Bleeding control: direct pressure first
sections.body:
Severe bleeding can kill in minutes, so it takes priority even over cleaning. There are three types: capillary (oozing, minor), venous (steady dark-red flow), and arterial (bright-red, spurting with the pulse — most dangerous). Steps, in order:
1. Protect yourself — wear gloves if available (bloodborne infection risk).
2. Apply firm DIRECT PRESSURE straight onto the wound with a clean cloth, gauze pad, or your gloved hand. This is the single most effective action for the vast majority of bleeding.
3. Press hard and hold continuously for at least 10 minutes without peeking — lifting to look disrupts the forming clot and restarts bleeding. Set a timer.
4. If blood soaks through, do NOT remove the first dressing (you tear off the clot); add more pads on top and keep pressing.
5. Elevate the injured limb above the level of the heart if no fracture is suspected, to reduce blood-flow pressure.
6. Once bleeding stops, secure a pressure dressing (pad + firm bandage) but not so tight it cuts off circulation — check that the skin beyond stays warm/pink and a pinched nail refills in <2 seconds.
Signs of dangerous blood loss (shock): pale, cool, clammy skin; fast weak pulse; rapid breathing; thirst; confusion; fainting. Lay the person down, keep them warm, and get emergency help. An adult has ~5 liters of blood; losing ~750 mL (~15%) starts to matter, and ~1.5–2 L is life-threatening.

sections.heading: Wound packing and tourniquets for life-threatening bleeding
sections.body:
When direct pressure alone cannot control severe bleeding from a limb or a deep junctional wound, escalate. WOUND PACKING (for deep wounds NOT on the chest, abdomen, or neck): press a clean gauze roll (or hemostatic gauze if available) firmly into the wound cavity, packing it tightly right down onto the bleeding source, then hold hard direct pressure over the packed wound for at least 3 minutes. The packing provides pressure at the actual source deep inside. TOURNIQUET (for life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure/packing cannot stop, e.g. a partial amputation or arterial spurt):
1. Place a commercial tourniquet — or an improvised one from a ~5 cm-wide strip of strong cloth plus a rigid windlass stick (never a thin cord/wire, which cuts) — ~5–7 cm (2–3 inches) ABOVE the wound, between the wound and the heart, but NOT over a joint (go above the joint if needed).
2. Tighten until the bright-red bleeding STOPS completely; it will hurt — that is expected. Half-measures worsen bleeding by blocking veins but not arteries.
3. Write the exact TIME of application on the tourniquet or the person's forehead. This is critical for the hospital.
4. Do NOT loosen or remove it once applied — leave that for medical professionals. A tourniquet can safely stay on for up to ~2 hours with low risk to the limb; the priority is the life over the limb.
Get emergency help urgently. Safety note: tourniquets are a last resort for otherwise-uncontrollable bleeding, not for minor cuts.

sections.heading: Cleaning and irrigation: removing contamination
sections.body:
After bleeding is controlled, cleaning prevents infection by physically removing dirt, debris and bacteria — the mechanical flushing matters more than any antiseptic. Steps:
1. Wash your hands and put on gloves.
2. Irrigate with a large volume of clean fluid under gentle pressure. Best is sterile saline, but potable (drinkable) tap water is well-supported and effective; if water is questionable, use water that has been boiled and cooled. Use roughly 50–100 mL of fluid per centimeter of wound length, more for dirty wounds.
3. Generate mild pressure (~5–8 psi) to dislodge debris: a 20–60 mL syringe with an 18-gauge catheter tip, or a plastic bag/bottle with a small hole, delivers about the right force. Too little pressure fails to clean; a firehose blast drives bacteria deeper and damages tissue.
4. Gently remove any visible embedded grit, gravel or splinters with clean/sterilized tweezers. Deeply embedded objects, or a large impaled object, should be left in place (they may be plugging a vessel) and dealt with by professionals.
5. Scrub the surrounding intact skin, not the wound bed itself.
What NOT to pour into the open wound: hydrogen peroxide, full-strength iodine, or alcohol — these kill healthy healing cells and slow recovery; reserve antiseptics (dilute povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine) for the intact skin around the wound. Clean water flushing is the workhorse. Do not use butter, dirt, cobwebs or other folk substances — they add infection.

sections.heading: Closure decisions and dressings
sections.body: Not every wound should be closed. CLOSING traps bacteria inside, so it is only appropriate for clean, fresh wounds. General guidance: clean, straight-edged cuts that gape open may be closed within roughly 6–24 hours of injury (sooner on the trunk, up to ~24 h on the well-supplied face). Small gaping cuts can be approximated with adhesive strips ('butterfly'/steri-strips) or skin glue after thorough cleaning, pulling the edges gently together. LEAVE OPEN (to heal from the bottom up, or for professional care): puncture wounds, animal or human bites, wounds older than ~24 hours, visibly dirty or infected wounds, and crush injuries — closing these risks trapping infection. Wounds needing stitches/professional closure: deep (fat or muscle visible), longer than ~1–2 cm and gaping, on the face or over a joint, bleeding that won't stop, or with damage to nerves/tendons (numbness, weakness). DRESSINGS keep the wound clean and support 'moist wound healing,' which heals faster and scars less than letting a hard scab form: (1) apply a thin layer of plain petrolatum or antibiotic ointment if available; (2) cover with a non-stick sterile pad; (3) secure with tape or a bandage; (4) change daily or whenever wet/dirty, cleaning gently each time. Keep the dressing dry when possible. A clean scab should not be picked off. For large or deep wounds, seek care rather than self-managing.

sections.heading: Recognizing and managing infection
